blocks.text: Post-Train a Model for Your Own Agent Harness with OpenHands and Snowflake

inlines.text: Post-Train a Model for Your Own Agent Harness with OpenHands and Snowflake

blocks.text: Written by
Graham Neubig at OpenHands, Karthik Ganesan at Snowflake, Tunji Ruwase at Snowflake

inlines.text: Graham Neubig at OpenHands, Karthik Ganesan at Snowflake, Tunji Ruwase at Snowflake

blocks.text: Published on
November 3, 2026
OpenHands × Snowflake AI Research

AI coding agents are increasingly being customized for specific development workflows. Developers configure system prompts, tools, skills, execution environments, and turn budgets to help agents work effectively within their repositories and engineering processes.

inlines.text: AI coding agents are increasingly being customized for specific development workflows. Developers configure system prompts, tools, skills, execution environments, and turn budgets to help agents work effectively within their repositories and engineering processes.

blocks.text: But there’s a disconnect: while the agent harness is customized for your workflows, the model powering it typically isn’t.

inlines.text: while the agent harness is customized for your workflows, the model powering it typically isn’t.

blocks.text: Most models are post-trained using general-purpose agent configurations that differ from the environments where they’re ultimately deployed. The result can be familiar problems: incorrect tool calls, ignored skills, unnecessary steps, or agents that exhaust their turn budgets before completing a task.

inlines.text: Most models are post-trained using general-purpose agent configurations that differ from the environments where they’re ultimately deployed. blocks.text: Developers can continue refining prompts and tools to address these issues, but there’s another option: post-train the model to perform better within the agent harness itself.

inlines.text: Developers can continue refining prompts and tools to address these issues, but there’s another option: post-train the model to perform better within the agent harness itself.

blocks.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a way to do this. The model attempts tasks within an agent environment, receives feedback based on the results, and updates its weights to improve performance.

inlines.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a way to do this. The model attempts tasks within an agent environment, receives feedback based on the results, and updates its weights to improve performance.

blocks.text: The challenge is that traditional RL frameworks often introduce their own agent loops, tool formats, and task structures. Developers must recreate their existing harness inside the training framework, introducing additional engineering work and potential differences between training and deployment.

blocks.text: OpenHands and Snowflake are addressing this gap by enabling developers to post-train models using their existing OpenHands agent harnesses.

blocks.text: With the OpenHands Agent SDK, developers can configure agents with their own prompts, tools, and skills. Tasks are defined using the open Harbor format, while Snowflake Cortex Training provides the GPU infrastructure for reinforcement learning.

blocks.text: That flexibility extends to post-training.

During training, every rollout is a real execution of your OpenHands agent. The system prompt, tools, skills, and execution limits are passed as configuration rather than recreated inside a separate RL framework.

inlines.text: During training, every rollout is a real execution of your OpenHands agent. The system prompt, tools, skills, and execution limits are passed as configuration rather than recreated inside a separate RL framework.

blocks.text: Part of your harness
How you set it

HARBOR_SKILL, one or more SKILL.md paths

MAX_TURNS, MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH
A fully custom agent
HARBOR_AGENT=my_package:MyAgent
Base model
MODEL (for example: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B)

The agent doesn’t need to know it’s being trained. It sends ordinary chat-completion requests, and a proxy between the agent and the model records the exact tokens the model produces on each turn. Those tokens become the training data: the model learns from its own outputs, while the prompts and tool results are excluded from the loss.

blocks.text: Let OpenHands run the training
Even with an existing agent harness, configuring and managing an RL training run involves several operational decisions.

inlines.text: Even with an existing agent harness, configuring and managing an RL training run involves several operational decisions.

blocks.text: Developers need to allocate GPUs, configure batch sizes and sequence limits, launch training jobs, monitor progress, troubleshoot failed rollouts, and release compute resources when training finishes.

inlines.text: Developers need to allocate GPUs, configure batch sizes and sequence limits, launch training jobs, monitor progress, troubleshoot failed rollouts, and release compute resources when training finishes.

blocks.text: The new cortex-training-rl skill in OpenHands/extensions automates much of this process.
Using OpenHands, developers can describe the training run they want, and the coding agent handles the setup and execution.

inlines.text: Using OpenHands, developers can describe the training run they want, and the coding agent handles the setup and execution.

blocks.text: For example, in OpenHands:

Use /cortex-training-rl to post-train Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on my Harbor tasks in ~/my-harbor-tasks/train and ~/my-harbor-tasks/eval with my agent's skill at ~/my-skill/SKILL.md, a 15-turn budget, for 50 steps.

blocks.text: Good to know
There are a few implementation details to consider when configuring training.

inlines.text: There are a few implementation details to consider when configuring training.

Training involves executing thousands of model-generated commands. Each rollout receives its own Snowflake Cortex Sandbox, and the training machine’s credentials are not exposed to the sandbox. This provides isolation between training infrastructure and agent execution.
The agent’s terminal executes each command in a fresh shell. The working directory persists between commands, but exported environment variables and background processes do not. The OpenHands
tool is not currently available during training, so agents must edit files through the terminal.
The launcher targets Hopper GPUs by default and uses FlashAttention 3. Other GPU configurations can be selected through the available settings.
